sentences.sentence: "Harkin Steak Fry."

Yes, that same Harkin Steak Fry that was once an essential event on the Democratic presidential calendar is now a glorified fundraiser, attended by a lot of Democrats, but one that could be easily ignored by the candidate who becomes the presumptive nominee this fall.

It is also a reflection of the Iowa Democratic Party's struggle to come to grips with the fact that it is no longer on the national stage, and the party's own state politicians are largely irrelevant to the rest of the country.
They are also struggling to adjust to the fact that the Democrats' last three presidential contenders — Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton and John Edwards — made the steak fry a non-event.
Obama didn't bother to show up at all.
Clinton brought husband Bill, but the former president made a short speech and left.
Edwards — whose campaign staff had originally made travel arrangements to fly back and forth from Des Moines, Iowa — bailed on the event altogether.
If the 2016 Democratic nominee wants to have a good time and raise some cash with a few thousand Iowans and party big-wigs, he or she could do it anywhere.
Why bother going to the steak fry?

And as the steak fry continues to lose its national luster, it seems reasonable to wonder why Iowa Democratic Party Chairman Scott Brennan would feel the need to spend $15,000 on a $100-a-head dinner with local elected officials, activists and members of the local press.
You have to give Brennan credit for at least recognizing the party's new reality, though.
He changed the name.
The "Harkin Steak Fry" will now be known simply as the "Iowa Democratic Party Steak Fry."

sentences.sentence: a BTR armoured personnel carrier and 10 troop trucks, said the town’s mayor, Pavel Zhebrivsky.
Another 20 tanks and 70 troop carriers were said to be in Donetsk, 43 miles away.
A Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman in Moscow said the tanks had been taken to Donetsk by a humanitarian convoy taking food to refugees fleeing the fighting in eastern Ukraine.
A Ukrainian military spokesman in Kiev confirmed that the tanks were on the streets of Snizhne.
‘They are ours now.
They belong to the Ukrainian army,’ Col Vladyslav Seleznyov said.
However, the separatists, who seized control of the region a few months ago, claimed the tanks were theirs.
‘There is a base of ours,’ said a rebel commander called Vladimir, who refused to give his surname.
‘The Ukrainian army attacked and destroyed it.
There are no Ukrainian tanks here.
If you want to see our tanks you’ll need to go to Donetsk.’
The Ukraine army also claimed to have destroyed a base in Rassypnoye, 20 miles away, where separatist troops were said to have taken control of an airfield.
This was unconfirmed and there were also reports that separatist forces had seized the town of Svitlodarsk, east of Donetsk, and the airport at Luhansk.
Russian propaganda is likely to fuel reports of its tanks crossing the border into eastern Ukraine.
It may also be a way of making the West think it has more of them there than it actually has.
Last week Russia sent a convoy of 200 lorries into eastern Ukraine carrying badly needed humanitarian supplies.
The West refused to endorse the move and criticised Russia for crossing the border without permission.

sentences.sentence: launch was postponed by three days because the weather forecast for the launch site had deteriorated.
This delay comes just a week after Nasa gave SpaceX the go ahead for a further contract – valued at over $1.6 billion – to send crews to the International Space Station.
The test launch and landing, known as an orbital test flight, is a crucial step in Elon Musk’s dream to open up space travel to a wide range of customers.

If the flight goes to plan, it will mean Musk’s company will be the first to launch and return a reusable spacecraft from orbit, with the potential to launch and land a spacecraft a dozen times a day.
The hope is that by allowing a rocket to land back on Earth rather than falling to the sea or a wasteland, the cost of space travel could be greatly reduced.
In a paper published in November this year, Nasa scientists estimated that if a space shuttle could be reused up to 50 times, the launch cost could be reduced by as much as 80 per cent.
The test flight was scheduled to see SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket send the Dragon cargo spacecraft to the International Space Station, where the craft will deliver supplies.
The spacecraft will then return to Earth and splash down off the coast of Florida, at which point the Falcon 9 rocket should attempt to land back on Earth on a platform in the Atlantic Ocean.
The flight will mark the 18th time a Falcon 9 rocket has launched from the historic Launch Complex 39A at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center.

This week, Abrams's investigative eye was cast on a 60-year-old case that rocked the tiny town of Tontogany.
"I can go and solve a genealogy problem for anyone," said the North Olmsted, Ohio, resident.
"You give me the name of someone you're trying to find, and I can find them."
Abrams is a licensed private investigator who has a knack for piecing together family histories and using the information to solve cases.
Some are criminal in nature, and others are civil suits.
Her clients range from a U.S. Customs agent to attorneys in family law disputes to private individuals, such as the person searching for a long-lost relative.
As Abrams tells it, someone would hire her to find a person's ancestors for a specific purpose.
"The client pays me to get the information, but not to disclose it," she said.
The attorney, for example, would present a picture of the man's family as evidence in a civil or criminal suit.
Or the client might need proof of kinship, such as the son of an Ohio man who was searching for his grandmother and wanted to inherit her estate.
His father had told him the story that he was born out of wedlock and then abandoned by his birth mother, but he could never prove it.
His curiosity led him to hire a genealogy expert.
Sure enough, Abrams tracked the man's birth mother down in Florida.
She is still alive today.
"It was such a great story," Abrams said.

'How can police expect the confidence of victims of abuse in Rotherham when they're so openly congratulating each other?'
Jim Andrews told the Sheffield Telegraph.
'It really is astonishing that the force has the time to hold an event to pat themselves on the back while other officers are working round the clock to bring down drug gangs in the borough.
In response to the criticism, Detective Superintendent Simon Homan, who chaired the awards, defended the decision to hold the ceremony.
'This is not a celebration of the past but looking forward to how we want to serve our community in the future,' he said.
'We had to make a decision whether we should proceed.
The feedback we received was that the ceremony should go ahead.'
On the same day South Yorkshire Police used its public Facebook page to draw attention to the event with a message about its policing awards.
'These awards recognise the outstanding work that police officers, staff and volunteers put in to making our communities safer,' it said.
The criticism comes less than two weeks after independent report by Professor Alexis Jay branded Rotherham Council's child protection efforts a 'disgrace'.
The review said at least 1,400 children had been sexually exploited in the South Yorkshire town between 1997 and 2013.
The victims were as young as 11 and were mainly white girls, with learning difficulties.

sentences.sentence: year, Danica didn't flinch when she was called in to work on the film set of "Mad Max: Fury Road" in the outback.
As her husband had told her countless times, his safety was their "number one priority."
"Whenever my husband leaves to work abroad, it's always difficult," said Danica.
"But I knew Paul would be surrounded by a lot of his old friends so it would be OK.
He wanted me to go and do something that made me happy, so I did."
During his time in Africa and Asia, Paul told her not to worry about the family finances.
"He knew I was working, and he said: 'Just worry about looking after the kids, I'll be OK,'" she said.
But Danica was shocked when she found out Paul had died while working in Mongolia.
Danica had a hard time digesting the news.
"I'd only just received an email telling me everything was OK, and then I got a call from Paul's boss asking me to contact the consulate because my husband was dead," she said.
"I was in absolute shock.
I needed someone to talk to, someone who had been in the same situation.
And I wanted to tell the story in my own way."
While Danica knew other families had been in a similar position, it was often a story told by people on the outside looking in.
She wanted to hear the same story from a mother who had been there.
That story was the beginning of "The One That Got Away."
"Paul was like a rock in the family.
He was the one who put the kids to bed, helped them with homework.
I was the one who was meant to be the softer parent, the one who was supposed to go and give the cuddles.
So Paul was the main provider, emotionally and financially," said Danica.
"Paul was in an accident at work, and we didn't know what happened.
